clinical_knowledge.topic: Live Insect Foreign Body (External Ear Canal) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Live Insect Foreign Body (External Ear Canal) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with terrifying buzzing and scratching sound and feeling of movement inside the ear after a camping trip. 24M camper presenting with extreme panic and loud buzzing in the right ear.
reference_soap.objective: Vital signs stable. Otoscopy confirms a live moth trapped inside the right external auditory canal; tympanic membrane intact, no canal laceration or bleeding.
reference_soap.assessment: Live insect foreign body, right external auditory canal, confirmed by otoscopy.
reference_soap.plan: Confirm the foreign body by otoscopy. Immobilize or kill the insect with warm mineral oil or 2% lidocaine before careful removal under direct visualization; avoid irrigation if tympanic-membrane perforation is suspected. Reinspect the canal and tympanic membrane after removal and arrange ENT care if extraction is unsuccessful, deeply impacted, or associated with injury.

teaching.diagnosis: Live Insect Foreign Body (External Ear Canal)
teaching.one_liner: A live insect trapped in the ear canal causes terrifying buzzing and a sensation of movement — the first step is immobilizing the insect (mineral oil or lidocaine) before extraction, since a struggling insect can cause pain and eardrum injury.
red_flags: Severe pain or bleeding — could indicate eardrum injury from the insect's movement

must_ask.say: What exactly do you feel or hear — buzzing, scratching, movement?

history.answer: Doctor, please help me! There's a terrifying buzzing and scratching sound inside my right ear, and I can literally feel something moving around in there.
It started about two hours ago while I was packing up my tent on a camping trip, and it is definitely in my right ear.
It feels like constant crawling, scratching, and intense, loud fluttering right against my eardrum.
It is not a sharp stabbing pain, but more of an intensely distressing, irritating ache that spikes whenever the insect flutters.
No, it just happened suddenly this morning at the campsite, so it hasn't been a lingering issue over multiple nights.
No, tugging on my earlobe, pressing in front of my ear, or chewing does not make the pain worse.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 128/82 mmHg, heart rate 88 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and temperature 36.8°C.
The patient appears visibly anxious and distressed, frequently touching his right ear, but is in no respiratory distress.
Otoscopy reveals a live moth fluttering within the right external auditory canal with an intact tympanic membrane and no canal laceration, bleeding, or pinna/tragus tenderness.
Whisper test shows mild conductive hearing reduction on the right side, with Weber lateralizing to the right ear and Rinne showing bone conduction greater than air conduction on the right.
Facial expressions are fully symmetric with normal forehead elevation, eye closure, and smile, and cranial nerves II through XII are grossly intact.
Oral cavity, dentition, and pharynx are clear without mucosal lesions, and temporomandibular joints are non-tender with normal range of motion.
No palpable preauricular or cervical lymphadenopathy, and the neck is supple without tenderness.
